cards.heading: The loudest possible whisper still cannot be heard
cards.narration: Could our universe have been born inside a black hole and kept its parent's spin like a birthmark? Think of a ceiling as the loudest a whisper could possibly be. We read all 4 published papers—the whole four-link chain—and calculated that ceiling. No observable signature survives. Even the loudest signal is about 10,000 to 100,000 times quieter than the best possible galaxy count, like a whisper buried under a stadium. The route stays closed. Here's how we got there.

cards.heading: The question is whether a baby universe keeps a birthmark
cards.narration: Picture a black hole as a cosmic nursery. Matter falls inward, but the story says the collapse opens into a new, expanding universe. That baby might inherit a birthmark: the direction its parent was turning. The glowing thread on screen is the proposed memory route. We will follow it through each paper and stop wherever a calculation stops. First, what could turn a crushing collapse into a bounce?

cards.heading: Paper 1 says spin twists spacetime
cards.narration: Picture spacetime—space and time joined—as cloth woven from tiny compass needles. A particle's spin is a built-in quantum property—a rule at nature's smallest scales—like one needle's direction. Einstein-Cartan gravity is Einstein's gravity extended to include spin. In that theory, all those tiny twists can twist spacetime itself. That spacetime twist is called torsion. Our illustration lights the twist only after the cloth appears. This paper contains no plots—the entire argument is equations. So how could that faint twist reverse a collapse?

cards.heading: Torsion acts like a spring at the bounce
cards.narration: Squeeze a spring and it pushes outward. At crushing density, torsion—the spin-made twist in spacetime—is proposed to push the same way. A negative torsion density means an outward effect, not less than nothing. Collapse then turns into a bounce, a change from shrinking to growing. Today's estimate is roughly a negative 1 sitting 70 places after the decimal point—like one whisper against an unimaginably loud room. The no-plots card stays beside our spring illustration. But how do we add up countless tiny spins?

cards.heading: The answer swings with how the spins are averaged
cards.narration: A stadium clapping together is thunder; random claps mostly cancel. The paper averages particle spins like a crowd forced onto one beat. A species simply means one kind of particle. It groups 6 neutrino species—6 kinds of nearly weightless particle—like six stadium sections clapping in step. If they act independently, the torsion estimate is exactly 6 times smaller—like cutting the same song to one-sixth volume. Those choices make the two labeled edges on screen. The printed value sits near the lined-up edge, so we carry both. What if a later correction changed the print?

cards.heading: The correction exists, but its words remain unread
cards.narration: A correction notice is like a sealed envelope we can see but cannot open. We can see the notice; its words remain paywalled. We quarantined the affected numbers, meaning we set them aside, and recomputed them ourselves. That stops an unread correction becoming a guess. With both edges carried, what does the next paper show?

cards.heading: Paper 2 draws a sharp cusp instead of a smooth turn
cards.narration: Imagine the same builder replacing a spring with a new engine. This newer paper uses fermion fields—the deeper ingredients matter particles are made from—as its torsion engine. Figure 1 is the paper's first window into the bounce. The scale factor is a ruler for the universe's size. Follow the glowing cursor like a ball rolling downhill: the ruler shrinks, reaches a sharp bottom, then grows. That pointed bottom is a cusp, not a smooth U-turn. And how hot does that sharp corner get?

cards.heading: The temperature spike reveals a family fight
cards.narration: Think of rival engines whose manuals reject each other. Figure 2 is the second window, a thermometer. The blue line spikes near the Planck scale, the extreme where tested classical rules run out. One quote says “violates the cosmological principle,” meaning the rule that the large-scale universe looks the same in every direction. Another calls the older foundation “not self-consistent.” Their bounce densities—the crush levels where they turn—differ by about 730 times, like bridge blueprints disagreeing on weight. The equations never stop collapse; the reversal is written in by hand. So what can the next paper pass on?

cards.heading: Paper 3 passes along mass, size, and heat—not rotation
cards.narration: Picture a black hole as a seed pod. Collapse inside the pod reaches the proposed bounce and opens into a baby universe. At fixed compactness—how tightly the starting matter is packed—the parent's mass enters the map on screen. The arrow leads to the baby's starting size and heat. This is the inheritance channel the papers actually calculate. This paper also contains no plots—the entire argument is equations. The parent's rotation arrow stays outside the map. So does any fingerprint survive for long?

cards.heading: The starting fingerprint quickly fades
cards.narration: Birth certificates list size, not life stories. Cited computer results say later growth follows a particle-creation dial—the setting for how quickly new particles appear—not starting size. Mass enters the start but leaves no claimed later fingerprint. The join is a sketch, not a weld. Horizon matching means calculating how the interior joins the black hole's one-way boundary; none is provided. The showcase numbers need a starting ball exactly 1 meter wide—about a doorway—and the paper never states that choice. Where, then, is the spin bridge?

cards.heading: Paper 4 offers one sentence where a spin bridge needs equations
cards.narration: A bridge needs beams, not a hopeful sign. A spin bridge needs an equation carrying the parent's rotation into the baby. Our shrinking-star illustration shows the newer collapse first. This paper contains no plots—the entire argument is equations. Then the lone source card appears. Across all 4 papers, no equation carries the parent's spin through the bounce; the collapse papers mention it in exactly 1 sentence: “It would still be valid for a more realistic gravitational collapse of an inhomogeneous and rotating fluid.” That line supplies no rotating model or axis calculation. So how loud could the missing bridge be?

cards.heading: The causality wall leaves only a ceiling
cards.narration: A skater pulls in, spins faster; the 10-solar-mass, spin-0.7 parent faces that extreme. Keeping its rotation demands motion 6.6 times 10 to the power 26 beyond light—billions of trillions past nature's red line. A uniform bounce means all regions collapse alike. Treatments mean rival engines. An order of magnitude means a tenfold step. Requiring the paper's uniform bounce caps inherited spin near 1 part in 10 to the power 27, with the treatment branches spanning roughly 1 order of magnitude. Picture one grain in a billion-by-billion-by-billion grain cube. And if a spinning parent can't make their bounce at all, there is even less to see. Would the bounce smooth lopsidedness?

cards.heading: The bounce neither smooths nor creates lopsidedness
cards.narration: Squeeze a balloon unevenly; one side bulges, the other flattens. Uneven squeezing is shear. Torsion, the spin-made spacetime twist, and shear change at the same rate as the universe changes size. The on-screen scale stays level. Their ratio, the comparison between them, is frozen. The bounce neither smooths nor creates lopsidedness. Any lasting memory depends on particle production—the creation of new particles—a step the papers assert but never derive. This is a condition, not a signal size. Can a real cosmic fossil hear anything this chain leaves behind?

cards.heading: Ancient helium cannot hear the torsion whisper
cards.narration: Think of helium as a fossil thermometer. Big-bang nucleosynthesis means light elements forming as space expanded. The plots compare elements, then set a helium ceiling. A stiff component is energy fading faster than radiation, light-like energy. At 10 megaelectronvolts, a particle-energy unit, this is first-minute heat. The ceiling allows up to 30 times radiation, like thirty buckets beside one. The torsion whisper is about 45 orders of magnitude smaller—forty-five tenfold steps, like one molecule beside Earth's oceans. Different signs; both vanish. Could perfect galaxy counting do better?

cards.heading: Even the most generous signal is 10,000 times below the floor
cards.narration: Flip many coins and heads never lands perfectly half; chance leaves a wobble. Even counting all 2 trillion observable galaxies—one vote each—that wobble remains. The counting floor is the quietest signal a perfect count could hear, not an instrument. Now turn every survival knob to maximum. The budget still lands about 10,000 to 100,000 times below that floor. A whisper beneath a stadium. The Planck regime is the extreme where quantum gravity—gravity's unfinished smallest-scale rules—should matter. One honest caveat: both bounces sit in the Planck regime treated classically, and the strict chain awaits external theorist review.

cards.heading: Every link returns to the same closed verdict
cards.narration: On screen, paper cards reconnect. The spring paper proposes a bounce, but its strength is not unique. The sharp-corner paper replaces that engine with an incompatible, inserted turn. The mass-map paper passes starting size and heat, not rotation. The collapse paper offers a lone unsupported line, not a bridge. Helium hears no whisper. Even the loudest stack remains about 10,000 to 100,000 times below the floor—a stadium-buried whisper. The strongest route ends at a ceiling. The ceiling says the route stays closed.
